name: Industry Use Cases
blurb: What AI is actually used for, industry by industry, with ROI, vendors, risks, and case studies.

metrics.source: US Census Bureau, Business Trends and Outlook Survey (national estimates)

questions.text: In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.)

During the next six months, do you think this business will be using Artificial Intelligence (AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.)

sectors.name: Accounting
sectors.blurb: Transaction classification, audit anomaly detection, close automation, and the shift from sampling to full-population testing, with AICPA, IMA, and benchmark sources.

sectors.name: Agriculture
sectors.blurb: Vision-guided spraying, yield prediction, and autonomous equipment at commercial scale, tracked through USDA ERS, FAO, satellite data providers, and the equipment and standards bodies.

sectors.name: Banking
sectors.blurb: Fraud detection and credit models are decades old. Generative AI in service and compliance is the new frontier, under Fed SR 11-7 model risk supervision.

sectors.name: Churches and Faith Organisations
sectors.blurb: Sermon prep, administration, and pastoral limits across hundreds of thousands of congregations, from Barna research and faith-tech platforms to Notre Dame ethics work.

sectors.name: Construction
sectors.blurb: Computer-vision safety monitoring, BIM clash detection, and autonomous site scanning, sourced from AGC, BuiltWorlds, and the proptech and contech trackers.

sectors.name: Defense
sectors.blurb: Decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing as programs of record. DIU as the commercial on-ramp. Free federal procurement data first, subscription analysts labeled.

sectors.name: Education
sectors.blurb: Tutoring systems, drafting assistance, and academic integrity policy from K-12 through university, with market tracking and this site's own course catalog.

sectors.name: Energy
sectors.blurb: Grid optimisation, exploration, and the datacenter power crunch that makes energy both an AI user and AI's binding constraint, from EPRI and DOE to the utilities and oilfield majors.

sectors.name: Government
sectors.blurb: Federal AI use inventories, GAO oversight, international readiness indexes, and the state legislatures writing AI law tracked on this site.

sectors.name: Healthcare
sectors.blurb: Imaging diagnostics, clinical documentation, and drug discovery, with the health-specific model benchmarks and KLAS and Rock Health tracking adoption.

sectors.name: Hospitality
sectors.blurb: Revenue management, service automation, and AI assistants as a booking discovery channel hotels now compete in, from Skift and AHLA to the distribution and restaurant tech vendors.

sectors.name: Insurance
sectors.blurb: Underwriting, claims triage, and fraud detection under active regulator supervision, with NAIC, AM Best, and the Evident insurance index.

sectors.name: Legal
sectors.blurb: Research, review, and drafting at scale, the citation-sanction lesson, and the benchmarks and trade bodies that measure legal AI accuracy.

sectors.name: Manufacturing
sectors.blurb: Predictive maintenance, machine vision on the line, and generative design, with A3 automation data, IoT Analytics, and NIST standards work.

sectors.name: Media
sectors.blurb: Generation tools transformed production while training-data litigation transformed the business relationship with AI; cross-linked to the lawsuit tracker.

sectors.name: Mining
sectors.blurb: Autonomous haulage and ore-body modelling in the sector that automated early, from USGS exploration data and Earth MRI to Rio Tinto, Komatsu, KoBold, and the AI-native explorers.

sectors.name: Nonprofits
sectors.blurb: Grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery on small budgets, with governance capacity as the constraint, from CEP and NTEN to Candid and the equity project.

sectors.name: Real Estate
sectors.blurb: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest AI and now federally regulated under FHFA and CFPB quality-control rules; plus valuation, leasing, and property-management platforms with methodology disclosed.

sectors.name: Retail
sectors.blurb: Demand forecasting, recommendation, and customer-service automation at volume, with NRF, Coresight, and IHL tracking the deployments.

sectors.name: Sports
sectors.blurb: Performance analytics, broadcast automation, and officiating assistance, from NCAA and NFHS governance to Hudl, Catapult, and the sports technology research network.

sectors.name: Transportation
sectors.blurb: Autonomous driving is the visible front; AI also runs freight matching, maritime navigation, transit, and aviation, from IMO and EASA to the trucking, shipping, and aviation majors.

analysis.body:
In the latest period, 23.8% of businesses reported using AI in the last two weeks, up from 17.3% in the first available period. The share fluctuated over the series, with a low of 17.2% and a high of 23.8%. The share answering no fell from 71.6% to 66.5%, and the do not know share moved from 11.1% to 9.7%.

Expectations for future AI use also rose. The share expecting to use AI in the next six months moved from 21.1% in the first available period to 27.6% in the latest period. The expected no share fell from 56.8% to 46.3%. The expected do not know share moved from 22.2% to 26.1%, with a low of 21.9% and a high of 26.5%.

In every period shown, the expected use share is higher than the current use share. In the latest period, current use stands at 23.8% while expected use stands at 27.6%. At the start of the series, current use was 17.3% and expected use was 21.1%. This persistent gap indicates that businesses anticipate adoption beyond what they currently report.

The do not know share for future use is much larger than for current use. In the latest period, 26.1% of businesses do not know if they will use AI in the next six months, compared with 9.7% who do not know about current use. This suggests considerably more uncertainty about future AI adoption than about present use. The expected do not know share rose from 22.2% to 26.1% over the period, while the current do not know share fell from 11.1% to 9.7%.

findings.body: The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey asks a representative sample of US firms every two weeks whether they used AI in the last two weeks - the closest thing the industry has to an official adoption statistic, shown live above. What the cross-sector reading adds: adoption is wildly uneven. The sectors on this site with the deepest sourced coverage - real estate, agriculture, mining, transportation - are not the sectors with the loudest AI marketing, and the sectors with the loudest marketing are not the heaviest measured users. Sector bodies that count deployments (A3 for robotics orders, NRF and Coresight for retail, AHLA for hotels, EPRI for utilities) consistently report deployment concentrated in a minority of large firms while the median firm is still piloting.
findings.heading: Adoption is measured, and the measurement disagrees with the hype in both directions

findings.body: Banking has supervised models since the Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 guidance in 2011; insurance regulators coordinate through the NAIC's model bulletin; and automated valuation models in real estate came under federal quality-control rules from FHFA and CFPB in 2024-2025, effective before most sectors had any AI rule at all. The pattern across the 21 sectors: where a prudential regulator already existed, AI arrived into a supervision framework, and the compliance conversation is about model risk management, not about whether rules apply. Where no such regulator exists, the governing pressure comes from the state legislatures tracked in this site's law database instead.
findings.heading: The regulated industries got AI rules before the AI boom

findings.body: Mining has run driverless haul trucks in production since the early 2010s - Rio Tinto's autonomous fleet is the canonical case - and agriculture ships vision-guided sprayers and autonomous tractors as commercial products from the major equipment makers, not as pilots. Maritime autonomy has an IMO regulatory code in development and aviation has an EASA AI roadmap. The finding that generalizes: autonomy matured fastest where the operating environment is bounded (a mine site, a field, a shipping lane) and slowest where it is open (city streets), which is why the robotaxi story and the autonomous-haulage story read a decade apart.
findings.heading: The physical industries automated earliest and quietest

findings.body: Healthcare has HealthBench for clinical answers; legal and accounting have the vals.ai evaluations built with the professions' own bodies; banking and insurance have the Evident indexes ranking named institutions on AI maturity. General model leaderboards tell a hospital or a bank nothing about their liability; the sector benchmark movement exists because the question that matters is no longer "which model is smartest" but "which system is safe for this regulated task", and every sector page here links its own measurement bodies.
findings.heading: Benchmarks are going sector-specific, because general benchmarks stopped answering the buyer's question

findings.body: Utilities use AI for grid optimization and demand forecasting (EPRI and DOE grid-modernization programs anchor that work), while at the same time datacenter load growth has made electricity the limiting input for the AI industry itself - the capex telemetry on this site tracks the same buildout from the spending side. No other sector sits on both sides of the ledger, and the interaction runs in both directions: AI demand is reshaping utility planning, and utility interconnection queues are reshaping where AI capacity gets built.
findings.heading: Energy appears twice: as an adopter and as the binding constraint

findings.body: The media sector's AI relationship is being negotiated in court: the training-data lawsuits tracked live in this site's lawsuit database are simultaneously licensing negotiations, and the settlements and rulings coming out of them are writing the de facto rules for how creative work enters training corpora. Media is thin on this page by design - two sourced points - because the substantive record is the docket, and it is cross-linked rather than duplicated.
findings.heading: In media, litigation is the industry structure

findings.body: Federal agencies publish AI use-case inventories, GAO audits them, and international indexes (Oxford Insights, OECD.AI, the Stanford AI Index) rank national readiness - while the same governments write the rules everyone above must follow, including the 2,400+ state bills in this site's law tracker. The three roles pull in different directions, and the tension is visible in the sources: the strongest federal accountability source, GAO's consolidated AI inventory, sits behind a bot wall this site declines to fake.
findings.heading: Government is adopter, referee, and scorekeeper at once

findings.body: Every one of the 153 sector points links a verified primary source: government and statistical programs first, then trade associations and standards bodies, then the operating companies' own published programs. Paywalled analyst estimates (Gartner, IDC, McKinsey), equity-fund marketing pages, and vendor vertical brochures are excluded on principle; sources that block automated verification (IEA, GAO's inventory, USDA's main site) are named as walled rather than quietly substituted. Where a number appears on a sector page, the page it came from still serves it.
findings.heading: What this coverage will not do

synthesis.body:
Across all 21 industries, the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey is the only consistent, recurring measure of AI use, and it asks a narrow question: in the last two weeks, did this business use AI in any of its business functions. The national series begins in September 2023 and is published biweekly. The latest national reading in this material is 23.8% answering Yes, against 66.5% answering No and 9.7% answering Do not know. Asked whether the business expects to use AI in the next six months, 27.6% said Yes, 46.3% said No, and 26.1% said Do not know. Those three numbers frame every sector below, because the sector figures are drawn from the same instrument and are not directly comparable to vendor surveys or market forecasts.

The sector-level spread is wide. Per the Census Bureau, Information sits highest at 49.0%, up from 43.5% in the prior period, and Professional, scientific, and technical services, the grouping that contains accounting and legal work, sits at 43.9%, up from 43.3%. Finance and insurance, which covers banking and insurance, is at 41.0%, up from 36.5%. Education is at 30.0%, down from 35.5%, and real estate and rental and leasing is at 29.6%, down from 31.9%. Healthcare and social assistance is at 25.5%, up from 24.7%, and arts, entertainment, and recreation is at 22.6%, up from 20.0%. Manufacturing is at 19.5%, down from 23.4%, and retail trade is at 16.5%, up from 15.5%. Construction is at 15.4%, down from 16.0%, and the Census Bureau's other services category, which covers religious organizations and much of the nonprofit sector, is at 15.0%, up from 13.7%. Transportation and warehousing is at 13.0%, up from 7.9%, utilities is at 11.8%, down from 16.4%, accommodation and food services is at 10.1%, up from 8.5%, and mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction is at 8.0%, up from 5.3%. Agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting is lowest at 6.2%, with the prior period suppressed. Defense has no Census adoption figure in this material at all, so no measured rate can be stated for it.

What AI is deployed for varies by sector, and the sources describe it in operational terms rather than as a single capability. In accounting and legal, the documented work is population-level anomaly detection over general ledger entries, agentic preparation of large datasets, and independent benchmarking of legal reasoning and search quality. In healthcare, the National Institutes of Health describes biomedical data across electronic health records, omics, imaging, and disease-specific datasets, and OpenAI's HealthBench was built with 262 physicians practicing in 60 countries and contains 5,000 realistic health conversations. In insurance, the NAIC lists underwriting, pricing, customer service, claims handling, marketing, and fraud detection, and notes AI may help insurers move from detect and repair toward predict and prevent. In manufacturing, the activity clusters around predictive maintenance, machine vision on the line, and generative design, with NIST supplying the common vocabulary through its Risk Management Framework and measurement work. In transportation, Aurora pairs professional drivers with the Aurora Driver on long-haul routes, Samsara sells AI-driven alerts and dash cam safety technology across 20,000+ operations, and C.H. Robinson applies AI to logistics orchestration. In media, the Associated Press uses AI to analyze video and create shotlists with all generated descriptions reviewed and edited by editorial staff, and it treats any generative AI output as unvetted source material.

Where vendors and money concentrate is visible unevenly. Legaltech Hub reports 1,416 solutions in its directory incorporating generative AI from 1,117 providers across 19 categories as of the end of September 2026. In real estate, JLL states it has invested more in AI technology than any other real estate company, and CREtech describes an event expecting 3,000 leaders, 150 speakers, and 20,000+ pre-scheduled 1:1 meetings. In sports, Hudl is described as the dominant platform for game film across high school, college, and pro programs, with Catapult and Kinexon as the primary wearable and tracking platforms at the NCAA and professional level. In agriculture, AgFunder reports global agrifoodtech funding hit $16.2 billion in 2025, almost flat versus the prior year at -3%. In energy, the World of AI's Data Centers section, drawing on the Department of Energy's 2024 LBNL report, records that datacenters consumed about 4.4% of US electricity in 2023, projected to reach 6.7 to 12% by 2028, with AI as the driver. In defense, the money trail is legible mainly through federal procurement data on SAM.gov, USAspending, and FPDS, with Govini, the Silicon Valley Defense Group, Janes, and Forecast International as the named analysts.

ROI evidence is the weakest part of the record, and the sources mostly say so. OpenAI reports that o3 outperforms other models including Claude 3.7 Sonnet and Gemini 2.5 Pro on HealthBench, that its frontier models improved by 28% on HealthBench in recent months, and that GPT-4.1 nano outperforms August 2024's GPT-4o despite being 25x cheaper. Samsara states 380,000+ accidents prevented. Climate FieldView states that farmers using FieldView seed scripts saw an average increase of +5 bu/ac compared to users who wrote their own scripts. Amperon claims accuracy up to 3x better than older methods. Against those, the accounting material notes that more than 9 in 10 senior finance leaders in a recent survey said they are under career pressure to demonstrate a return on agentic AI investment, and the government material reports no ROI figures for government AI deployments. For most sectors, including construction, hospitality, nonprofits, sports, mining, and defense, the excerpts report no measured return at all.

The regulatory posture splits into binding rules, sector supervision, and voluntary ethics. The sharpest binding rule in the material is the interagency automated valuation model rule adopted by the CFPB, OCC, FRB, FDIC, NCUA, and FHFA, requiring quality control standards, random sample testing and reviews, and protections against data manipulation for AVMs used in mortgage collateral decisions. Banking and insurance inherit the Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 model risk management guidance from 2011, and the NAIC expects insurers to explain how AI is used in underwriting, pricing, marketing, or claims decisions while keeping humans in the loop. In transportation, EASA's Artificial Intelligence Roadmap 2.0 sets out safety and ethical considerations for AI in aviation, and the IMO adopted a new International Code of Safety for Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships in May 2026, effective 1 July 2026, requiring a MASS Safety Certificate. In media, Article 50 of the EU AI Act requires providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio, image, video or text to mark outputs in a machine-readable format. In government, this site's tracker counts 6,049 artificial intelligence bills across 53 jurisdictions, with only two states passing a broad law reaching consequential decisions across sectors, Colorado in CO SB189 and Texas in TX HB149. In healthcare, the World Health Organization's guidance sets out six consensus principles and recommends governance holding public and private stakeholders accountable to healthcare workers and affected communities. In manufacturing and mining, the posture is standards-led rather than rule-led, through NIST and through safety, tailings, emissions, and tax transparency reporting.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a few consistent readings. First, measured adoption is real but uneven, and in several sectors the latest reading moved down rather than up, including education, real estate, manufacturing, construction, utilities, and the broader services grouping that contains accounting and legal, so peer pressure is not a reliable signal. Second, the documented deployments are mostly back-office, analytical, and assistive rather than autonomous, and where autonomy exists it is gated by certification regimes, as in aviation and maritime, or by safety cases, as in autonomous trucking. Third, independent evaluation exists in some sectors, through HealthBench's physician-written rubrics, Artificial Analysis, KLAS Research, Vals AI, and STRN's peer-reviewed quality framework, and its absence elsewhere should be treated as absence rather than reassurance. Fourth, the recurring constraints the sources name are data quality and inventory accuracy in retail, incomplete agency inventories in government, grid and interconnection limits in energy, and governance capacity and budget in nonprofits, not model capability. Where the sources are silent, on sector-specific ROI, on vendor market shares, and on the content of guidance pages that failed to load, this material does not fill the gap.
